title: The one-item case
idea: MEET (thinking). A list with exactly one item is an edge case: loops still work, but 'compare to the next one' ideas can go wrong.

exercises.prompt: You total a list with a loop. With ONE item, the total is...
options: Just that one item — the loop runs once
exercises.explanation: One item means the loop runs once, adding that item. Summing a single-item list is safe and correct.

exercises.prompt: You find the highest value starting 'best = scores[0]'. With ONE score, the answer is...
options: That one score — it is trivially the highest
exercises.explanation: With one score, best starts as that score and nothing beats it. The single item IS the highest — correct.

exercises.prompt: A single-item list is still safe for 'start best at the first item' — there's a first item to read.
exercises.explanation: Yes. One item means there is a scores[0], so starting best there works. The empty case is the one that breaks it.

exercises.prompt: Averaging a list with ONE item (say [8]) gives...
exercises.explanation: Total 8, count 1, average 8.0. One item is safe for averaging because count is 1, not 0.

exercises.prompt: When might a single-item list actually cause trouble?
options: If your plan compares each item to the NEXT one — there's no next item
Never — one item is always safe
exercises.explanation: Plans that look at pairs ('compare each to the next') have no pair when there's only one item. That's the risky single-item case.

exercises.prompt: Which plans are SAFE on a one-item list? (Select all that apply.)
options: Compare each item to the one after it
exercises.explanation: Total, average, and max all work with one item. Only 'compare each to the next' struggles — there's no next item.

exercises.prompt: Match each list size to the max-finding result for [7] versus bigger lists.
exercises.explanation: Empty breaks max-finding; one item is trivially the max; several items need the real comparison.

exercises.prompt: Checking the one-item case is a good way to make sure your loop logic isn't secretly assuming 'many items.'
exercises.explanation: Yes. If a plan only works with several items, the single-item test exposes the hidden assumption.

exercises.prompt: REVIEW: the three list sizes worth checking as edge cases are...
options: empty, one item, and many items
exercises.explanation: Empty, one, and many are the three sizes to think through. Each can behave differently in a plan.

options: Check the one-item case — it's safe for totals and max, but breaks 'compare to the next'
One item is the same as empty
exercises.explanation: A single-item list is usually fine, but it exposes plans that assume a 'next' item. Always think it through.
